title: while(flag){} never terminates: JVM caching/hoisting, volatile fix
shortTitle: Why does while(flag){} never terminate without volatile?
keyPoints: Without volatile, the JIT compiler may hoist the flag read out of the loop, caching it in a CPU register.
The hoisted form becomes 'if (flag) while(true) { }', which never re-reads the variable from memory.
This is a legal JIT optimization under the Java Memory Model because there is no happens-before relationship.
volatile prevents hoisting: every read must go to main memory, so the loop sees the updated value.
This bug is difficult to reproduce in debug mode because the JIT does not optimize uncompiled code.
Alternative fixes include synchronized reads, but volatile is cheaper and simpler for flags.

s1_definition.oneliner: Without volatile, the JIT compiler can hoist a flag read out of a loop, caching it in a CPU register, so the loop never sees updates from another thread and runs forever.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **JIT hoisting** – the JIT compiler sees that a variable is not modified within the loop body. It legally optimizes `while(flag) { work(); }` into `boolean cached = flag; while(cached) { work(); }`. The variable is read once and cached in a register.
- **Register caching** – the CPU register holds the stale value (e.g., `true`). Even when another thread writes `false` to main memory, the loop thread never reads main memory again.
- **JMM legality** – without a happens-before relationship (volatile, synchronized, or Lock), the JVM is not required to guarantee cross-thread visibility. The optimization is legal.
- **volatile fix** – declaring the variable `volatile` inserts a memory barrier that prevents hoisting and register caching. Every read must fetch from main memory.
s1_definition.analogy: A bank security guard checks the "OPEN" sign once when their shift starts. The guard writes "OPEN=true" on a sticky note (CPU register) and keeps checking the sticky note all day. When the manager flips the sign to "CLOSED" at 5PM, the guard still reads "OPEN" from the sticky note and never locks the doors. volatile forces the guard to look at the actual sign every time, not the sticky note.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Without volatile (JIT hoisting):

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Worker Thread                             │
  │                                           │
  │ boolean cached = running;  // read ONCE   │
  │ while (cached) {           // register    │
  │     work();                // forever!    │
  │ }                                         │
  │                                           │
  │ Main Memory: running = false              │
  │ (worker never reads it again)             │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

  With volatile:

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Worker Thread                             │
  │                                           │
  │ while (running) {  // volatile read       │
  │     // reads main memory EVERY iteration  │
  │     work();                               │
  │ }                                         │
  │                                           │
  │ Main Memory: running = false              │
  │ (worker sees it on next iteration!)       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Without volatile, the JIT compiler can hoist a flag read out of a loop, caching the value in a CPU register. The loop becomes `while(true)` because the thread never reads from main memory again. Even though another thread writes `false` to main memory, the loop thread is stuck with the stale `true` in its register.

This is a legal optimization under the Java Memory Model. Without a happens-before relationship, the JVM is not required to guarantee cross-thread visibility. volatile fixes this by inserting a memory barrier that prevents hoisting and forces every read to access main memory.

This bug is particularly insidious because it does not manifest in debug mode or with small loop counts. The JIT only hoists after compiling hot code, so the bug appears only in production.

Remember one sentence: without volatile, the JIT may cache a loop flag in a CPU register, causing an infinite loop that only volatile or synchronized can fix.
